# Abstract

`joinme_mix()` extends the nested multivariate longitudinal model in JoiNMe
with a finite latent-progress distribution. The extension deliberately leaves
the observation models, covariance regression, survival likelihood,
and association transformations unchanged. It reuses the prediction machinery
with the same mixture prior for newly sampled latent effects. The ordinary
centred distribution of selected *standardised* random effects is replaced by
a \(G\)-component location--scale mixture. The selected coordinates are
two-dimensional by default, subject to the available dimension of the
random-effect block.

Discrete class indicators are integrated out exactly. Stan therefore samples a
continuous posterior and generated quantities recover conditional class
probabilities for each subject or marker. Random-effect blocks with the same
allocation unit share a class: subject effects and covariance-regression
effects share an subject allocation, while marker effects and estimated
marker weights share a marker allocation. A combined request consequently
defines \(G\), not \(G^L\), classes.

This chapter states the statistical model, explains how latent classes change each
association channel, distinguishes class-centre and marginal trajectories, and
sets out the assumptions required for a defensible interpretation.

# The nested longitudinal model

Let \(i=1,\ldots,n\) index subjects, \(d=1,\ldots,D\) index markers, and
\(j=1,\ldots,n_{id}\) index measurements. Conditional on its linear predictor,
the response follows the marker-specific family

\[
Y_{idj}\mid \eta_{id}(t_{idj}),\boldsymbol\psi_{idj}
\sim \mathcal F_d\!\left\{
g_d^{-1}\bigl(\eta_{id}(t_{idj})\bigr),\boldsymbol\psi_{idj}
\right\}.
\]

The nested predictor is

\[
\eta_{id}(t)
=
\underbrace{\boldsymbol x_{id}(t)^\top\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{population}}
+
\underbrace{\boldsymbol z_i(t)^\top\boldsymbol u_i}_{\text{subject}}
+
\underbrace{\boldsymbol z_d(t)^\top\boldsymbol v_d}_{\text{marker}}
+
\underbrace{\boldsymbol z_{id}(t)^\top\boldsymbol w_{id}}_
{\text{subject-by-marker}}.
\]

The four terms have deliberately separate interpretations.

- \(\boldsymbol\beta\) describes the population trajectory.
- \(\boldsymbol u_i\) describes movement shared by all markers of subject
  \(i\).
- \(\boldsymbol v_d\) describes a deviation common to marker \(d\).
- \(\boldsymbol w_{id}\) describes the remaining trajectory of marker \(d\)
  within subject \(i\).

The implementation uses non-centred random effects:

\[
\boldsymbol u_i=L_u\boldsymbol z_{u,i},\qquad
\boldsymbol v_d=L_v\boldsymbol z_{v,d},
\]

where the Cholesky factors contain the fitted scales and correlations. The
subject-by-marker effect is

\[
\boldsymbol w_{id}
=
\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol r_w)L_i\boldsymbol z_{w,id}.
\]

Here \(L_i\) is an subject-specific lower-triangular factor produced by the
covariance regression and \(\boldsymbol r_w\) contains any time-scale
adjustments.

# Covariance regression as a random-effect block

Write \(m=1,\ldots,M_{\mathrm{cov}}\) for the free entries required to construct
\(L_i\). For the full lower-triangular model,
\(M_{\mathrm{cov}}=Q(Q+1)/2\); for an independent covariance model,
\(M_{\mathrm{cov}}=Q\). The linear predictor for entry \(m\) is

\[
\ell_{im}
=
\alpha_{L,m}
+
\boldsymbol x_{\mathrm{cov},i}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta_{L,m}
+
\lambda_{L,m}z_{L,im}.
\]

For each packed lower-triangular coordinate \(m\), \(\lambda_{L,m}\) is one
non-negative scalar loading. The collection
\(\boldsymbol\lambda_L\in\mathbb R_+^{M_{\mathrm{cov}}}\) is stored as a
vector; equivalently, its action is the diagonal mapping
\(\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\lambda_L)\boldsymbol z_{L,i}\), not a dense
loading matrix. In an ordinary fit with \(z_{L,im}\sim N(0,1)\),
\(\lambda_{L,m}\) is the residual standard deviation of \(\ell_{im}\) before
the diagonal link or off-diagonal partial-correlation transformation.

Diagonal predictors pass through `softplus` or `exp`, as selected by
`vcov_diag_link`. Off-diagonal predictors are mapped through the fitted
partial-correlation construction. `class_type = "corr"` acts only on
off-diagonal correlation coordinates, whereas `class_type = "vcov"` may
select any lower-triangular coordinate of \(\boldsymbol z_{L,i}\). Both describe
latent classes of subject differences in covariance structure, rather than assigning a
mixture directly to the innovations \(\boldsymbol z_{w,id}\).

When coordinate \(m\) receives a class-specific distribution and
\(z_{L,im}\mid C_i=g\sim D(\mu_{gm},s_{gm})\), the latent contribution becomes
\(\lambda_{L,m}z_{L,im}\). It consequently has class-specific location
\(\lambda_{L,m}\mu_{gm}\) and distributional scale
\(\lambda_{L,m}s_{gm}\). Hence \(\lambda_{L,m}\) remains a common
coordinate-specific loading, whilst \(\mu_{gm}\) and \(s_{gm}\) describe
class differences. For Student-\(t\) or Laplace components, “scale” here is
the distribution's scale parameter rather than necessarily its standard
deviation.

This distinction matters. A covariance class need not move the conditional
mean trajectory, because \(\boldsymbol w_{id}\) remains centred within that
class. It changes the dispersion, correlation, covariance association, and the
marginal response trajectory whenever the inverse link is non-linear.

# Finite latent-progress distribution

## Selected coordinates

For every class-eligible block \(b\), let
\(\boldsymbol a_{r,b}\) be the selected standardised coordinates for allocation
unit \(r\). By default, JoiNMe selects coordinates 1 and 2. If only one
coordinate exists, the one-dimensional model is retained. The choice can be
made explicit through `class_dimensions`.

For class \(g\), coordinate \(k\) has location \(\mu_{gk}\) and positive scale
\(s_{gk}\). Conditional on class,

\[
a_{r,bk}\mid C_r=g
\sim
D_\nu(\mu_{gk},s_{gk}),
\]

independently over the selected standardised coordinates. The family
\(D_\nu\) follows `shrinkage`:

\[
D_\nu =
\begin{cases}
t_6, & \texttt{shrinkage}=0,\\
\text{Laplace}, & \texttt{shrinkage}=1,\\
\mathcal N, & \texttt{shrinkage}=2.
\end{cases}
\]

The diagonal component scale is intentional: the established Cholesky factors
continue to carry the random-effect correlation structure on the realised
scale, while the mixture describes displacement and dispersion on the
standardised latent-progress plane.

## Mixing proportions

Let

\[
\boldsymbol\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_G),\qquad
\boldsymbol\pi\sim
\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\boldsymbol\alpha_\pi).
\]

For one allocation unit with selected vector \(\boldsymbol a_r\), the
marginal density is

\[
p(\boldsymbol a_r)
=
\sum_{g=1}^G
\pi_g
\prod_{k\in\mathcal K_r}
D_\nu(a_{rk};\mu_{gk},s_{gk}).
\]

Stan evaluates its logarithm as

\[
\operatorname{log\_sum\_exp}_{g=1}^G
\left[
\log\pi_g
+
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K_r}
\log D_\nu(a_{rk};\mu_{gk},s_{gk})
\right].
\]

No discrete parameter is sampled. This exact marginalisation is essential for
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and also retains uncertainty when classes overlap.

## Allocation domains

The public class types and their allocation units are:

| class type | latent quantity assigned to classes | allocation unit |
|---|---|---|
| `"subject"` | \(\boldsymbol z_{u,i}\) | subject \(i\) |
| `"corr"` | off-diagonal coordinates of \(\boldsymbol z_{L,i}\) | subject \(i\) |
| `"vcov"` | lower-triangular coordinates of \(\boldsymbol z_{L,i}\) | subject \(i\) |
| `"marker"` | \(\boldsymbol z_{v,d}\) | marker \(d\) |

Blocks in the same row domain are concatenated inside one component density.
For example,

\[
p(\boldsymbol z_{u,i},\boldsymbol z_{L,i})
=
\sum_{g=1}^G\pi_g\,
p_g(\boldsymbol z_{u,i})p_g(\boldsymbol z_{L,i}).
\]

There is one subject class probability vector, not separate subject and
covariance labels. If both allocation domains are selected, the domains
share \(\boldsymbol\pi\), \(G\), and the component labels, but probabilities
are reported separately because an subject is not a marker.

# Prior replacement and weighted analyses

The ordinary JoiNMe prior is evaluated first. For every class-specific coordinate,
the implementation subtracts its ordinary standardised density and adds the
finite-mixture density. This density-ratio construction changes precisely the
selected distribution and does not place a second prior on top of the original
one.

Formula-scoped random-effect weights continue to apply. If subject \(i\)
has random-effect weight \(q_i\), the selected component log density and the
removed ordinary log density are both multiplied by \(q_i\). This preserves
the established weighted-analysis convention.

The component scale prior is

\[
s_{gk}\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(1).
\]

## Scale decomposition and posterior geometry

The component scale is defined on a standardised latent coordinate, before the
ordinary random-effect transformation. For a covariance-regression coordinate,
for example,

\[
z_{L,im}\mid C_i=g\sim D(\mu_{gm},s_{gm}),\qquad
\ell_{im}=\cdots+\lambda_{L,m}z_{L,im}.
\]

The likelihood therefore encounters the class-specific distributional scale
through the product \(\lambda_{L,m}s_{gm}\). The analogous subject and marker
quantities pass through \(L_u\) and \(L_v\). Priors and information in other
coordinates distinguish the factors, but data may learn the product much more
strongly than its decomposition. Posterior compensation between a large
ordinary scale and a small component scale, or conversely, then creates a long
continuous ridge. Intercept ordering removes class-label permutation; it does
not remove this scale ridge.

This distinction is important for computation and interpretation. Low E-BFMI,
persistent energy, small adapted step sizes and long Hamiltonian trajectories
can arise even when the mixture density, threading and simulation coordinate
map are correct. `diagnosis()` consequently reports chain-specific energy
behaviour, the posterior correlation between ordinary and component scales,
and exploratory correlations between energy and low-dimensional block
summaries. These correlations describe posterior geometry rather than proving
that one parameter caused a sampling warning. The direct
\(\operatorname{Exponential}(1)\) prior regularises the component scale but
does not algebraically identify the likelihood decomposition.

Under the default `class_ordering = "intercept"`, Stan declares only the
first selected random-intercept location
\((\mu_{11},\ldots,\mu_{G1})\) as an `ordered[G]` vector. Selected slope and
other location coordinates receive unrestricted standard Normal priors. Thus
the labels are identified by progression level without requiring progression
rates to have the same order. If no selected coordinate is an intercept, this
rule imposes no location order.

`class_ordering = "probability"` instead imposes
\(\pi_1<\cdots<\pi_G\) on the baseline probabilities. Formula slopes remain
unrestricted, so covariate-dependent probabilities may cross away from the
zero-covariate reference point. `class_ordering = "none"` imposes neither
location nor probability ordering.

Class probabilities may depend on allocation-unit covariates. With class
\(G\) as reference,

\[
\Pr(C_j=g\mid X_j)
\propto
\pi_g\exp(X_j^\top\gamma_g),\quad g<G,
\qquad
\Pr(C_j=G\mid X_j)\propto\pi_G.
\]

`formulaClass` constructs \(X_j\); the intercept is omitted because
\(\boldsymbol\pi\) already supplies the baseline probabilities. A named list
may give separate `subject` and `marker` formulae. A list of exactly \(G\)
formulae instead gives a distinct predictor to every class, using a compact
coefficient vector containing only the terms requested by that class. Because
class-specific formulae need not share a natural low-to-high interpretation,
their default `class_ordering` is `"none"` unless it is supplied explicitly.
The Dirichlet concentration and Normal coefficient scale are supplied through
`jm_prior(class_probability = ..., class_regression = ...)`.

# Marker weights

For an active weighted association term \(a\), marker \(d\) has

\[
\omega_{ad}^{\mathrm{eff}}
=
\omega_{ad}^{(0)} + z_{\omega,ad}.
\]

If `shared_marker_weights = TRUE`, active current-value and current-slope terms
refer to one common set. If it is `FALSE`, every active weighted term has its
own set. These weights retain their ordinary JoiNMe prior and are not a
latent-progress class type.

# Survival submodel and association interpretation

For cause \(k\), the hazard is

\[
h_{ik}(t)
=
h_{0k}(t)
\exp\left\{
\boldsymbol w_i(t)^\top\boldsymbol\gamma_k
+
A_i(t)
\right\}.
\]

The association predictor may contain the following channels.

- `cv_mean` and `cs_mean` use the population plus subject trajectory.
- `cv_marker` and `cs_marker` use the marker and subject-by-marker
  deviation.
- `cv_total` and `cs_total` use the sum of mean and marker parts.
- `corr` and `vcov` use summaries reconstructed from \(L_i\).

For weighted marker channels, the transform is applied marker by marker before
the weighted average. A class-specific association trajectory follows the same
order:

\[
A_{ig}^{\mathrm{cv,total}}(t)
=
\alpha_{\mathrm{cv,total}}
\frac{1}{D}
\sum_{d=1}^{D}
\omega_{ad,g}^{\mathrm{eff}}\,
f_a\!\left\{\eta_{id,g}^{\mathrm{total}}(t)\right\}.
\]

Class-specific `corr` and `vcov` displays reconstruct \(L_i\), its covariance,
and the requested covariance summary at every posterior draw. They are not
obtained by applying a label to a pooled covariance curve.

For a marginal association trajectory, the ordering of operations follows the
hazard model: draw within class, construct the mean, marker or total feature,
apply its fitted transform, aggregate marker contributions, and only then
average over within-class draws. In general,
\(\operatorname E\{f(A)\mid C=g\}\neq
f[\operatorname E\{A\mid C=g\}]\).

# Posterior class probabilities

For subject-indexed blocks,

\[
\Pr(C_i=g\mid\boldsymbol a_i,\Theta)
=
\frac{
\pi_g p_g(\boldsymbol a_i)
}{
\sum_{h=1}^G\pi_h p_h(\boldsymbol a_i)
}.
\]

The same expression applies to marker-indexed blocks. Generated quantities
save the probability vector for every posterior draw. `posterior_class()`
reports the posterior mean as `Estimate`, the posterior standard deviation as
`Est.Error`, the 95% credible interval and the available chain diagnostics.
The maximum-probability
label is a convenient summary only. It should not replace the probability
vector when allocations are uncertain.

For dynamic prediction, let \(\mathcal H_i(t_c)\) denote the new subject's
longitudinal history up to conditioning time \(t_c\). The prediction programme
samples their latent effects conditionally on that history and reports

\[
\Pr\{C_i=g\mid \mathcal H_i(t_c),\Theta\}
\propto
\pi_g\,
p_g(\boldsymbol a_i)\,
p\{\mathcal H_i(t_c)\mid\boldsymbol a_i,\Theta\}.
\]

Computationally, the observation likelihood is evaluated by the established
dynamic-prediction reducer. A density-ratio adjustment then subtracts the
ordinary standard-Normal density for the selected coordinates and adds the
draw-specific fitted mixture. Subject and covariance-regression coordinates
enter the same component log density, so their conditional allocation remains
shared. Marker effects use the marker allocation domain. No discrete class
parameter is sampled.

# Class-specific longitudinal estimands

`mean_per_class` evaluates the fixed-effects trajectory plus the centre of
every class-specific block that enters the longitudinal location. For subject
and marker classes this is, schematically,

\[
m_{id,g}^{\mathrm{centre}}(t)
=
g_d^{-1}\!\left[
\boldsymbol x_{id}(t)^\top\boldsymbol\beta
+
\boldsymbol z_i(t)^\top L_u\boldsymbol\mu_{u,g}
+
\boldsymbol z_d(t)^\top L_v\boldsymbol\mu_{v,g}
\right].
\]

`marginal_per_class` draws from the fitted component distribution before
applying the inverse link and summarises those values across posterior draws:

\[
m_{id,g}^{\mathrm{marginal}}(t)
=
\operatorname E_g
\left[
g_d^{-1}\{\eta_{id,g}(t)\}
\mid\Theta,\mathcal D
\right].
\]

The two coincide under an identity inverse link when the remaining random
effects are centred. They differ for non-linear inverse links and when
within-class dispersion is appreciable.

Covariance and marker-weight classes require careful reading. A marker-weight
class changes the survival association but not the longitudinal trajectory.
A covariance class changes the distribution of subject-by-marker
departures; its centre need not change the conditional longitudinal mean.
Use `type = "covariance_class"` to inspect the class-defining covariance
profiles directly.

# Longitudinal-only model

If both event inputs are omitted, `joinme_mix()` creates a private event-design
scaffold so the common design builder can be reused. Stan receives zero event
indicators and zero integration intervals. Consequently,

\[
\ell_{\mathrm{survival}}=0
\]

exactly, and the posterior is based only on the longitudinal likelihood and
priors. Association terms are not admitted in this mode. Longitudinal
posterior prediction, posterior predictive checking,
MCMC plots, random-effect extraction, and class summaries remain available;
event discrimination and event plots correctly report that no event process
was fitted.

# Identifiability and interpretation

A fitted finite mixture does not by itself establish a biological taxonomy.
The following checks are part of a responsible analysis.

1. Inspect posterior class probabilities rather than only modal labels.
2. Check whether adjacent class-location intervals are meaningfully separated.
3. Inspect divergent transitions, effective sample sizes, \(\widehat R\), and
   trace plots for all mixture parameters.
4. Compare scientifically credible values of \(G\); do not choose \(G\) solely
   because it produces visually distinct curves.
5. Use posterior predictive checks within markers and, where appropriate,
   within high-probability classes.
6. Examine sensitivity to `class_probability`, `class_regression`, the chosen
   `formulaClass`, and `shrinkage`.
7. Treat a very small class cautiously: it can represent a genuine subgroup,
   an outlier accommodation mechanism, or an insufficiently regularised tail.

# Computational structure

The mixture adds \(G-1\) free mixing-proportion coordinates and \(2GK\)
location--scale parameters, where \(K\) is the total number of selected
coordinates. Allocation indicators do not enlarge the parameter space.
Evaluation cost grows approximately linearly with \(G\), the number of selected
coordinates, and the number of natural allocation units.

The existing `reduce_sum` likelihood remains unchanged. Mixture density
corrections are evaluated in the model block after ordinary priors and before
the threaded longitudinal-survival likelihood. Generated quantities recover
class probabilities and expand component locations back into their original
random-effect blocks for R summaries and plots.

# Reproducible reporting

A scientific report should state:

- the fitted \(G\);
- selected class types and coordinate indices;
- the component family chosen through `shrinkage`;
- the Dirichlet, location and scale priors;
- whether marker weights were shared;
- whether survival contributed to the likelihood;
- posterior class sizes with uncertainty;
- class-specific locations, scales and substantive curves;
- convergence and posterior predictive diagnostics; and
- sensitivity to alternative plausible class counts and priors.

The fitted object's `mixture` field and `summary()` output retain these details.
